results.evidence: Post gives directive legal instruction: 'If your jurisdiction allows it, request confirmatory testing on the original sample' — phrased as a command to take procedural action.

Every decision-action section includes proximate attorney redirects ('your attorney will need this,' 'Worth exploring with your attorney,' dedicated 'Questions Worth Exploring With Your Attorney' section).

Post describes general patterns ('Eight months of clean tests followed by one positive is a very different pattern') without rendering judgment about the specific reader's case strength or likely outcome.

Post recommends specific procedural step: 'If your jurisdiction allows it, request confirmatory testing on the original sample' — recommending a procedural action rather than explaining what confirmatory testing is.
Post does not touch immigration consequences (deportation, visa, DACA, green card) at all, so immigration-specific redirect is not triggered.
Post does not assert any collateral consequences (firearms, voting, housing, licensing) that would require statutory attribution.
Only general categories mentioned (NA, AA, SMART Recovery, Refuge Recovery are support-group categories, not recommended legal service providers or firms).
No first-person plural recommendations appear; the post consistently uses 'your attorney' rather than 'we recommend' or 'we advise.'
Second-person scene-setting ('You are sitting in the probation office') is direct reader framing, not a hypothetical presented as a real case that could be confused with actual facts.
Post consistently frames knowledge as enabling the reader to work with an attorney ('Questions Worth Exploring With Your Attorney,' 'Your attorney will need this'), not as replacing representation.
Post uses general qualifiers throughout: 'Most jurisdictions,' 'typically,' 'varies by state and by the probation office policy,' 'often results in.'
Outcome language is hedged with 'often' and 'typically' ('often results in increased treatment intensity,' 'that argument often works'); no guarantees of specific legal outcomes.

Legal strategies like cross-reactivity defense and challenging immunoassay reliability are presented without attribution to any named case, statute, scholar, or attorney — sources referenced only vaguely as 'published forensic toxicology research.'
No contradictory legal claims appear within the post; statements about graduated sanctions, standards of proof, and judicial discretion are internally consistent.
No ImNotAnAttorney.com products (Case Decoder, Intelligence Brief, etc.) are mentioned in the post.

Opening names fear well ('You relapsed. You failed a UA.'), but 4 of 6 H2s are topical: 'Immunoassay vs. Confirmatory Testing — The Science', 'What Judges Actually Consider at a Drug Test Violation Hearing', 'Questions Worth Exploring With Your Attorney', and 'The Bigger Picture' — none tell the reader what they GET.
GC-MS, IOP, and immunoassay are defined inline, but 'revocation' and 'chain of custody' are used repeatedly without inline definitions; paragraphs stay under 4 sentences.

Before the first H2 the only pre-section content is 'Stop. Breathe. One failed test is not the end' — reassurance, not a concrete 5-minute action block; the first real 'right now' action is buried inside the second H2 section.

Every decision point leads with a default: 'Enrolling in treatment before the hearing — not after — is the single strongest move you can make' and 'If you relapsed — enroll in treatment immediately. Not after the hearing. Now.'

'Questions Worth Exploring With Your Attorney' presents 10 unranked numbered items, and 'What You Can Do Before the Hearing' contains 7 unranked bolded action items with no 'start with these' priority grouping.
This post uses the system-decoder-post pattern — decoding how drug testing science and judicial discretion actually work behind the violation process.

Scary framings are consistently paired with action, e.g. the 'revocation becomes likely' for continued-use category is immediately followed by treatment enrollment guidance, and no section closes on fear without a paired move.
Zero blame language detected — 'You relapsed' is descriptive not moralizing, and throughout the post the person is separated from the situation with no 'you should have' or 'if you had' patterns.

Opens by validating fear ('your brain is now doing the math'), middle reduces unknowns (immunoassay science, judge factors), closes on agency: 'You are going to get through this. Start with treatment. Everything else follows from there.'
No tables, only H2 headings used, key actions are bolded — but 'What Judges Actually Consider' and 'What You Can Do Before the Hearing' both run 500-600+ words before the next H2.

Four H2 sections have strong shareable bolded sentences (e.g. 'An immunoassay tells you something looks like a drug — a GC-MS tells you what it actually is.'), but 'Questions Worth Exploring With Your Attorney' and 'The Bigger Picture' lack any bolded screenshot-worthy sentence.

All 5 FAQ answers start with the direct answer (no hedging preamble), stay within 2-4 sentences, and read in peer-support voice rather than institutional — e.g. 'Self-reporting almost always helps. Judges distinguish between defendants who come forward and those who get caught.'
